The reasoning that the Maclaurin coefficients must tend to 0 because the radius of convergence is 1 is flawed. A power series can have a radius of convergence 1 while its coefficients approach a non‑zero limit, e.g. \(1/(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^{n}\).  

Here \(f(x)\) has a simple pole at \(x=1\), the nearest singularity to the origin. The residue at this pole determines the dominant term of the series.  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{x=1}f(x)=\lim_{x\to1}(x-1)f(x)=\frac{(2025+1)\ln(2026)}{(1-2)(1-3)}=\frac{2026\ln2026}{2}=1013\ln2026.
\]

Since \(\displaystyle\frac{1}{x-1}=-\frac{1}{1-x}=-\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^{n}\) for \(|x|<1\), the contribution of this pole to the Maclaurin coefficients is \(-1013\ln2026\) for every \(n\). The remaining analytic part of \(f\) yields coefficients that decay to 0, so the overall coefficients satisfy  

\[
d_{n}\;=\;\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}\;\longrightarrow\; -1013\ln2026\neq0 .
\]

Thus the proposed limit \(0\) is incorrect.  

**VERDICT: REJECT**
